summary:
East Java stands under the national framework of Indonesia, a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. East Java has no provincial carve-out from this framework.

Physical risk is carried by the national regime rather than by any East Java-specific rule. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman, with Amnesty International stating the gathering violated no law. The Diplomat's August 2026 reporting is national and does not describe East Java specifically.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger anywhere in Indonesia, East Java included. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Documents and status: Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, so a trans visitor travelling on a foreign passport with a changed marker is entering a jurisdiction whose own standard of legal gender change is far stricter. Same-sex couples have no recognised legal relationship of any kind, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Indonesian law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection on those grounds.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller in Indonesia. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him; Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

East Java specifics are thin but concrete on one point: nothing in East Java civil law barred authorities from placing the trans woman Isa Zega in a women's prison facility by identity, and with no anti-discrimination framework there is no statutory basis on which to contest such a placement. A trans visitor detained in East Java therefore faces custody conditions determined by local practice alone.
tangentialFactors:
Two provinces outside East Java go further than the national code. Aceh and South Sumatra criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions; Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors, and two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship there in February 2025. Those rules do not travel with a visitor into East Java, but they indicate the direction of provincial legislation elsewhere in Indonesia.

Attitudes and the protection machinery are unfavourable. A 2025 Pew survey found 93% of Indonesians call homosexuality morally unacceptable. Indonesia voted against the independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity at the UN Human Rights Council in 2016, 2022 and 2025. The one countervailing datapoint is a Constitutional Court ruling of 14 December 2017 in which 5-4 justices rejected a petition to criminalise gay sex; the ruling narrowed a proposed expansion rather than creating a protection.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change in Indonesia requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and identity documents carry only 'male' or 'female' markers. There is no third-gender or X descriptor available.

No national law prohibits discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no hate-crime enhancement for offences motivated by those grounds. Same-sex couples hold no recognised legal relationship, with no associated rights around inheritance, hospital access or next-of-kin status.

Residents live under the October 2025 presidential decree that classifies LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat, and under continuing police action against LGBT gatherings; the 22 June 2025 villa raid near Bogor produced 75 arrests for an event Amnesty International said broke no law. Online platforms carrying LGBTQ content have been blocked, and a bill to prohibit such content online was under discussion in 2025.

Within East Java, the placement of the trans woman Isa Zega in a women's prison facility by identity proceeded without any civil-law bar and without an anti-discrimination framework to challenge it, illustrating how custodial decisions are made on local practice rather than on a statutory rule.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources disagree on the penalty for the 2022 penal-code provision on sex outside marriage: the national framework summary states up to two years' imprisonment, while the Wikipedia record gives up to one year. The discrepancy is unresolved here and both figures should be treated as provisional.

The Isa Zega case is recorded only as an outcome concerning prison placement. The date, the charges, the facility and any subsequent litigation are not sourced in this inventory and remain unresolved.

No source in this inventory documents East Java-specific enforcement: no raids, prosecutions, canings, refusals of entry, visa conditions or facility refusals are recorded as having occurred in East Java. Whether East Java has enacted provincial religious bylaws affecting LGBT people, and how those would apply to foreign visitors, is not addressed by the available sources.

Whether a trans visitor's foreign documents are accepted as presented at East Java ports of entry, and how Indonesian authorities resolve mismatches between passport marker and presentation, is not sourced; the inventory states only the domestic legal-gender standard.
